title: How to Bless Your Children
excerpt: Your children are listening for one thing underneath everything else: whether you delight in them. Blessing is how you say it out loud, on purpose, again and again.
body:
There is an ancient practice nearly lost in modern parenting: the spoken blessing. Throughout Scripture, fathers laid hands on their children and spoke words over their lives. Jacob blessed his sons. Jesus took children in his arms and blessed them. The practice assumes something we have forgotten, that words spoken over a child have weight, that a parent's blessing leaves a mark, and that children are waiting, often their whole lives, to hear it.

Many adults are still listening for a word their father or mother never spoke. You can break that pattern. You can be the parent who says it.

## What a blessing actually is

A blessing is not flattery and not a performance review. It is a parent speaking, with intention, that this child is loved, seen, and delighted in, apart from anything they have achieved. It says: I am glad you exist. I see who you are. I am for you. God is for you.

The model is the Father's word over Jesus at his baptism: "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased." Notice the timing. This was spoken before Jesus had preached a sermon, healed anyone, or gone to the cross. The delight came first, before the work. That is the order a blessing follows. You delight in your child before they have earned it, because that is how God's love runs, and a child who receives love that way grows up able to give it.

## Touch, words, and a future

A full blessing has a few simple parts, drawn from the old patterns. There is meaningful touch, a hand on the shoulder, an arm around them, the child held while the words are spoken, because the body remembers what the ears might forget. There are spoken words of love and high value, said out loud and to their face. And there is a word picturing a good future, a parent's confidence that God has good things ahead for this child.

It can be as simple as this, at bedtime, hand on their head: "You are my son. I love you. I am proud of who you are becoming. God made you for good things, and I cannot wait to see them. The Lord bless you and keep you." That last line is Aaron's blessing from Numbers, spoken over Israel for three thousand years. You can speak it over your child tonight.

## Bless the being, not just the doing

Most of what children hear from us is about their doing. Good job, nice work, you did well, you did poorly. The blessing is different. It speaks to their being, to who they are rather than what they produced. A child fed only on praise for performance learns that love is earned and conditional, and they spend their lives auditioning. A child who is blessed for simply being theirs learns that love is given, which is the only soil a real life grows in.

So bless the things that are not achievements. Their kindness. Their courage. The particular way they see the world. The fact that they are yours. Tell them you would choose them again. This is the love that does not depend on the report card, and it is the love that holds when the report card is bad.

## Make it a rhythm

A blessing spoken once is a gift. A blessing spoken as a rhythm becomes the ground a child stands on. Build it into something that already happens, the way family worship attaches to a meal. Bless them at bedtime. Bless them as they leave for school. Bless them on birthdays with something longer and more particular. Let your children grow up so used to hearing that they are loved and delighted in that they could not point to the day it started, only know it was always true.

The family devotions and seasonal resources at /family/devotions can help you build this into the year. But the words are yours to say, and your voice is the one your child is listening for.

## This week

Tonight, put a hand on your child and say a blessing out loud. Keep it simple: I love you, I am glad you are mine, I see who you are becoming, God has good things for you. Use Aaron's words if you have none of your own. Then do it again tomorrow, and the night after, until it becomes the thing your child knows without remembering when they learned it. You are answering, in advance, the question they will carry their whole lives: am I delighted in? Make sure the answer is yes, and make sure they heard it from you.
